title: 1 Kings
subtitle: Solomon's glory and a kingdom torn in two
lead: 1 Kings begins with King David old and cold in bed, and a fight over who will take his throne. Solomon wins it, asks God for wisdom, and builds the LORD a temple in Jerusalem. At its dedication the glory of the LORD fills the house like a cloud. For a few chapters Israel is at peace, rich, and famous among the nations.

Then the story turns. Solomon's many wives turn his heart to other gods, and after his death the kingdom splits in two: Israel in the north under Jeroboam, and Judah in the south under David's heirs. The book judges every king by one question, whether he was loyal to the LORD alone. Its last chapters belong to the prophet Elijah, who faces King Ahab, Queen Jezebel and the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel and asks Israel, "How long will you limp along on two crutches?"
facts: Not named. Jewish tradition (Bavli Bava Batra 15a): the prophet Jeremiah wrote Kings. Most critical scholars: part of the Deuteronomistic History, written or edited in the late 7th century BC and completed in the exile, from sources it names, such as the Scroll of Solomon's Deeds (11:41) and the records of the kings of Israel and of Judah (14:19, 29).
Set about 970–850 BC, from David's last days to the death of Ahab and the reign of his son Ahaziah. Kings as a whole ends after 561 BC (2 Kings 25:27), so it reached its final form in the exile.
Jerusalem and its temple; Shechem, Bethel, Tirzah and Samaria in the north; Mount Carmel, Horeb, Zarephath in Phoenicia, and Ramoth-gilead; with Egypt, Tyre, Sheba and Aram (Damascus) on the edges.

Historical narrative built on a framework of king-by-king summaries, with lists of officials and building records (4; 6–7), a long prayer (8:23–53), and prophetic stories (Ahijah, the man of God from Judah, Elijah, Micaiah).

Hebrew. The Greek Septuagint (called 3 Kingdoms) differs a great deal: it adds long passages about Solomon (after 2:35 and 2:46), arranges chapters 4–11 and 20–21 differently, and tells Jeroboam's rise twice (12:24a–z).
22 chapters, 816 verses. 1 and 2 Kings were one book in Hebrew; the Greek calls this book 3 Kingdoms (3 Reigns), and the Vulgate 3 Kings.

audience.to: Israelites who knew how the story ended. 1 Kings is the first half of one book, Kings. That book closes with Jerusalem burned, its people in Babylon, and the captive king Jehoiachin released from prison in 561 BC (2 Kings 25:27–30). So in its final form the book was written for Judeans in exile, or just after, who had lost the land, the temple and the throne. It also points readers to older records they could check (11:41; 14:19, 29) and notes things that remain "until today" (9:13; 12:19). Earlier forms of the book may have had other first readers, such as Judah under King Josiah in the late 7th century BC.
audience.why: To explain why the kingdom that reached its height under Solomon split in two and set out on the road to ruin. The book judges every king by one standard: did he worship the LORD alone, at the one place he chose, and keep his law, as David did? Solomon's prayer at the temple (8:46–53) already pictures Israel carried off as captives and turning back to God in the enemy's land. For exiles, that prayer was their own. The prophets in the book, Ahijah, the man of God from Judah, Jehu son of Hanani, Elijah and Micaiah, speak words that always come true. That tells readers that God's word, not the king's power, rules history. Knowing the readers changes the reading. Solomon's glory is not simply praised but shown as the high point before a fall. Elijah's lonely stand against Baal speaks to people tempted to worship the gods of their captors.
views: Jewish tradition says the prophet Jeremiah wrote Kings (Bavli Bava Batra 15a). On this view the book was written for Judah in its last days and in the first years of exile. Its writer was a prophet who had warned of the fall, using court records and the memories of the prophets' disciples.
A first edition for Josiah's Judah

Frank Moore Cross argued that a first edition was written under King Josiah (640–609 BC), to support his reform. The man of God's word naming Josiah (13:2) and the steady charge against the high places fit this view. So do notes such as 8:8, which speaks of the ark's poles as still in place "until today" and seems to come from before the temple fell. The first readers were people in Jerusalem being called back to one temple and one God, with hope in David's line.
The Deuteronomistic History, written after the fall

The Deuteronomistic History is the long history from Deuteronomy to Kings, written in the language of Deuteronomy. Martin Noth argued that one author wrote the whole of it after 586 BC, probably in Judah. He wrote to show that the disaster was just, because kings and people broke the covenant. The Göttingen school, scholars who followed Rudolf Smend at the University of Göttingen, sees several layers of editing after the fall. On these views the first readers were Judeans after the fall, asking why it happened and whether there was any way back.
Older prophet stories from the north

Many scholars think the Elijah and Micaiah stories were first told in northern Israel, among groups of prophets, before they were taken into the history. Their first hearers were people in the north under Ahab, faced with the worship of Baal.

lenses.name: History as told
lenses.desc: The traditional reading, Jewish and Christian: the book records Solomon's reign (about 970–931 BC) and the divided kingdoms from court annals it names (11:41; 14:19, 29), with prophets as God's witnesses. Jewish tradition credits Jeremiah with writing Kings (Bava Batra 15a).

lenses.name: Critical
lenses.desc: Most scholars read Kings as the last part of the Deuteronomistic History, written or edited in the late monarchy and the exile, judging each king by Deuteronomy's demand for one place of worship. They debate how large Solomon's kingdom really was, and how much of the Elijah stories is older prophetic legend.

lenses.name: Ancient records
lenses.desc: More of 1 Kings can be checked against outside sources than any earlier book: Shishak's raid (14:25) on the Karnak relief, Omri and Ahab in the Mesha Stele and Assyrian annals, Ahab's chariots at Qarqar (853 BC), and the gates and palaces dug at Hazor, Megiddo, Gezer and Samaria. Archaeologists disagree about what these finds prove.

lenses.name: Jewish tradition
lenses.desc: The rabbis read Solomon as both the wisest king and a warning, and Elijah as the prophet who never died, who comes to every circumcision and Passover table and will announce the Messiah (Malachi 4:5). The Temple dedication prayer (chapter 8) shapes Jewish prayer toward Jerusalem.

lenses.name: Christian
lenses.desc: The New Testament sees Jesus as 'greater than Solomon' (Matthew 12:42) and the true temple (John 2:19–21), and John the Baptist as coming with 'Elijah's spirit and power' (Luke 1:17). Elijah appears with Moses at the Transfiguration, and James holds up his prayer for rain (James 5:17–18).

authorship: Traditional view: Jeremiah and the prophets

The Talmud says that Jeremiah wrote the book of Kings (Bavli Bava Batra 15a). Kings and Jeremiah share much language, and 2 Kings 24:18–25:30 is repeated almost word for word in Jeremiah 52. Chronicles names prophetic records for Solomon's reign, by Nathan, Ahijah and Iddo (2 Chronicles 9:29), and Kings itself points readers to the Scroll of Solomon's Deeds (11:41) and the records of the kings of Israel and of Judah (14:19, 29). Notes such as "until today" (8:8; 9:13; 12:19) show a writer living after the events and working from older records. Traditional readers take the prophets' stories as eyewitness memories handed on by their disciples.

Since Martin Noth (1943), most critical scholars read Kings as the last part of one history running from Deuteronomy through 2 Kings, written to explain the fall of Israel and Judah by the standard of Deuteronomy: one God, one place of worship, and a king who keeps the law. Frank Moore Cross and his followers see a first edition under Josiah (late 7th century BC), which ends in hope, and a second in the exile; the Göttingen school sees layers added in the exile by historical, prophetic and legal editors. Inside the history scholars find older sources: the end of the Court History (1–2), administrative lists (4), a temple building record (6–7), royal annals, and cycles of prophet stories about Ahijah, Elijah and Micaiah, some of them perhaps first told in northern Israel.

Readers such as Jerome Walsh, Iain Provan, Peter Leithart and Robert Alter read 1 Kings as carefully built narrative: Solomon's reign arranged in a ring around the temple, ironies that undercut the king's glory, and prophets whose word always comes true. Many notice that the narrator praises Solomon openly in chapters 3–10 while planting small signs of the fall told in chapter 11.

sections.b:
The text page beside each chapter can show several translations. Only the one you pick is loaded.

Plain English

A fresh rendering made for this site from the Hebrew Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex), at about an 8th-grade reading level. Each verse was drafted from a word-by-word gloss of the Hebrew, then checked against other English versions and redrafted wherever it followed one of them too closely. Key terms match the rest of the site: YHWH is "the LORD" and Adonai YHWH "Lord GOD" (2:26); YHWH tseva'ot is "the LORD of Armies" (18:15); hesed is "loyal love" (3:6; 8:23); nagid is "ruler" (1:35); the law's chuqqim, mitzvot, mishpatim and edot are "rules," "commands," "rulings" and "decrees" (2:3); and nokhri is "foreigner" (8:41). Solomon's prayer (8:23–53) is set as prayer, and short poems such as 8:12–13 and the northern cry of 12:16 are set in poetic lines. Measurements are given in cubits, as in the Hebrew, with feet and meters in the notes. Chapters 4 and 5 follow English numbering: Hebrew 5:1–14 is English 4:21–34, and Hebrew 5:15–32 is English 5:1–18.

The Hebrew and the Greek 3 Kingdoms

The Greek Septuagint of this book, called 3 Kingdoms, differs from the Hebrew more than almost any other historical book. It adds two collections of short notes about Solomon after 2:35 and 2:46, lacks 6:11–14, puts the palace (7:1–12) after the temple's bronze work, places Solomon's poem (8:12–13) after the prayer with a note citing "the Book of the Song," tells Jeroboam's rise a second time (after 12:24), and puts Naboth's vineyard (21) before the Aramean wars (20). Scholars disagree about whether these differences preserve an older Hebrew text or are Greek-era rewriting, so the Plain keeps the Hebrew and shows the Greek in the variants. It follows the Greek only where the Hebrew seems damaged, as in the "bottom" level of the side rooms (6:8). Which Greek matters too: in 1:1–2:11 and in chapter 22 the main Greek manuscript, Codex Vaticanus, was revised toward the Hebrew (the "kaige" revision), and the Lucianic manuscripts are the better witness to the original Greek. Chronicles retells much of chapters 3–10, 12, 14–15 and 22, and small fragments of Kings were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls (4QKings, 5QKings, 6QKings).

Other translations

The Berean Standard Bible (2023), the King James Version (1611/1769), the American Standard Version (1901), Young's Literal Translation (1898) and the World English Bible can be shown for comparison.

The book has three movements. Chapters 1–11 are the reign of Solomon: the struggle for the throne (1–2), the gift of wisdom and the glory of the kingdom (3–4), the building and dedication of the temple at the center (5–8), the height of wealth and fame (9–10), and the fall, when his wives turn his heart and God promises to tear the kingdom away (11). Chapters 12–16 tell of the divided kingdom. Each king is introduced with a set formula: when he began to reign, counted by the years of the king in the other kingdom, how long he reigned, often his mother's name, and whether he did what was right or evil in the LORD's eyes. Northern kings are measured against "the sin of Jeroboam," his golden calves, and southern kings against David. Chapters 17–22 slow down to tell stories of prophets, above all Elijah, in the reign of Ahab, and the book ends in the middle of the story, which continues in 2 Kings.

More of 1 Kings can be compared with outside evidence than any earlier book. The Egyptian king Shishak (Sheshonq I) left a list of conquered towns at Karnak that matches his raid in 14:25–26. The Moabite Mesha Stele (about 840 BC) names Omri as the king who oppressed Moab, and the Assyrian Kurkh Monolith lists "Ahab the Israelite" with 2,000 chariots at the battle of Qarqar (853 BC), a battle Kings does not mention. Excavations at Samaria found Omri's and Ahab's palace and carved ivories like those of Ahab's "ivory house" (22:39). Solomon is harder to check. Traditional scholars such as Kenneth Kitchen take the lists and building reports as archival records from a real 10th-century kingdom. Low-chronology scholars such as Israel Finkelstein, and the minimalists, date the great gates and palaces of Hazor, Megiddo and Gezer to the 9th century and see Solomon's empire as a later ideal. A middle view, held by Amihai Mazar, William Dever and others, accepts a real but modest kingdom and an enlarged picture of its glory. The reigns of the kings also raise a long-standing puzzle, because the totals for Israel and Judah do not quite agree; scholars such as Edwin Thiele and Gershon Galil explain the gaps by co-regencies and different ways of counting years.

sections.h: How Jews and Christians read 1 Kings
sections.b: In Jewish tradition 1 Kings belongs to the Former Prophets, and many of its chapters are read as haftarot beside the Torah portions: David's old age beside Abraham's (1:1–31 with Genesis 23–25), David's last words beside Jacob's (2:1–12 with Genesis 47–50), Solomon's judgment beside Joseph's (3:15–4:1 with Genesis 41–44), the temple chapters beside the building of the tabernacle, and Elijah on Carmel beside the golden calf (18 with Exodus 32); the dedication of the temple is read on Sukkot and Shemini Atzeret (8:2–21; 8:54–66). The rabbis held Solomon in honor as author of Scripture yet weighed his sins; the Mishnah names Jeroboam and Ahab among the kings who have no share in the world to come (Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:2). Elijah, who never died (2 Kings 2:11), became the herald of the Messiah, welcomed with a cup at every Passover Seder and a chair at every circumcision. Christians read Solomon's peace and the temple as pointing to Christ, "something more than Solomon" (Matthew 12:42), and see in Elijah a pattern for John the Baptist (Luke 1:17). Jesus cites the widow of Zarephath (Luke 4:25–26), Paul the seven thousand who did not bow to Baal (Romans 11:2–4), and James Elijah's prayer for rain (James 5:17–18).

spec.title: Claude's theory: a book about listening
spec.body: My own reading of the whole book: 1 Kings is built around the Hebrew verb shama, "hear" or "listen." Solomon begins by asking for "a heart that listens" (3:9). His great prayer asks God again and again to listen from the heavens and forgive (8:30–52), and God answers that he has heard (9:3). Hiram and the queen of Sheba come because they have heard of Solomon (5:1; 10:1). Then the kingdom breaks because Rehoboam "would not listen to the people" (12:15). In Elijah's time the LORD does not speak in the wind, the quake or the fire, but in "a sound of thin silence" (19:12), and Micaiah, the one prophet who will not echo the king, begins, "So listen to the LORD's word" (22:19). I suggest that the book measures each king by whether he listens, to God, to the prophets and to his people, and that its turning points are moments of hearing or refusing to hear. Scholars often note the theme of hearing in Solomon's dream and prayer; reading the whole book through it is my own proposal.

A young king, Solomon, sits on a raised wooden throne in an open hall with one hand lifted to stop a guard. The guard holds a short sword over a small baby lying on a cloth. One woman kneels with her arms reaching toward the baby, pleading; a second woman stands apart with folded arms and a hard face. Courtiers watch from both sides.

Style: sketched by hand onto an old rolled parchment scroll. Sepia and iron-gall ink linework with charcoal shading, red-ochre and yellow-ochre pigment like Lascaux cave paintings, simple register lines like an ancient Near Eastern frieze, and a few bold flat shapes of deep blue in the manner of modern paper cut-outs. Visible parchment grain, uneven hand-drawn lines, soft torn irregular edges that fade into the parchment. No frame, no rectangular border, no sharp corners, no lettering. Wide horizontal composition, 3:2.

reading: The standard critical commentary, strong on history, the ancient Near East and the Hebrew and Greek texts.
Marvin A. Sweeney, I & II Kings (Old Testament Library, 2007)
A critical commentary attentive to the book's editions and to Jewish interpretation.
A close literary reading of the book's structure and storytelling.
A short evangelical commentary that reads Kings as a carefully crafted, critical history of the monarchy.
Peter J. Leithart, 1 & 2 Kings (Brazos Theological Commentary, 2006)
A theological reading in the Christian tradition, alert to typology and the temple.
Israel Finkelstein and Neil Asher Silberman, David and Solomon (2006)
The low-chronology case that the biblical picture of Solomon's kingdom grew over time; read beside Mazar or Kitchen for the other side.
